lesson.summary: Python reads almost like English, which is why it is a great first language.

content.text: **Python** is one of the world's easiest and most popular programming languages.
It powers websites, data science, AI, automation scripts and even games. Big companies and small startups both use it every day.
A Python program is just a list of instructions that run from top to bottom. The `print()` function shows a value on the screen:
Text in Python goes inside quotes. Both "double" and 'single' quotes work.

challenge.intro: Welcome to your first Python program! The code is already written for you.
steps: Press the **Run Code** button to execute it
You should see "Hello Python!" appear in the output
challenge.starterCode:
# Run this code to see the result:
print("Hello Python!")

reference.title: print()
reference.body: Shows one or more values in the output, separated by spaces.

lesson.summary: Notes in your code that Python ignores.

content.text: A **comment** starts with `#`. Python skips everything after it on that line, so comments are notes for humans.

content.code:
# This line is ignored
print("This line runs")  # a note at the end

content.text: Good comments explain *why* the code does something, not what every line does.

challenge.intro: The program prints two lines, but only one of them should run.
steps: Turn the second `print` into a comment by adding `#` in front of it

reference.title: # comment
reference.body: Everything after # on a line is ignored by Python.

lesson.summary: Use what you learned so far.

content.text: Time to put `print()` and comments together. No new ideas, just practice.

challenge.intro: Write a program that introduces you.
steps: Add a comment above it that says what the program does

lesson.solution:
# Introduce myself
print("I am learning Python")

reference.title: print()
reference.body: Shows a value in the output.

lesson.summary: Give a value a name so you can use it again.

content.text: A **variable** is a name that points to a value. You create one with `=`:
Read `=` as "is now". The name goes on the left, the value on the right.
Use a variable when you need the same value more than once.

challenge.intro: Store your favourite language in a variable and print it.
steps: Create a variable `language` with the value `"Python"`
Print the variable (not the text directly)

reference.title: Assignment
reference.body: name = value creates or updates a variable.

lesson.summary: What a valid, readable variable name looks like.

content.text: Names can use letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit. Python uses `snake_case` for multi-word names.

challenge.intro: Fix the variable name so the program runs.
steps: Rename `user name` to `user_name` on both lines

content.text: Assigning to an existing name replaces its value.

challenge.intro: A learner finished a lesson. Update their XP.

reference.title: Reassignment
reference.body: x = x + 1 reads the old value, then stores the new one.

content.text: Python has `int` for whole numbers and `float` for decimals. Numbers never go in quotes.

challenge.intro: Print how many days are in 3 weeks.

reference.title: int and float
reference.body: 7 is an int, 7.0 is a float.

content.text: `//` divides and drops the remainder, `%` gives the remainder, `**` raises to a power.

content.text: Real programs mix variables and arithmetic. Let us total a bill.

challenge.intro: Three notebooks cost 120 each and a pen costs 45.

content.text: A **string** is text in quotes. `+` joins strings and `*` repeats them.

challenge.intro: Build a greeting from two variables.

content.text: Put `f` before the quotes and wrap values in `{}`. Python fills them in.

streak = 7
print(f"{name} has a {streak} day streak")
